title: Ziba's Gifts, Shimei's Curses, and Ahithophel's Counsel
summary: As David flees, Ziba meets him with supplies and claims that his master Mephibosheth has stayed behind hoping to regain Saul's kingdom, and David hastily gives Ziba all Mephibosheth's property. At Bahurim, Shimei of Saul's clan curses David and pelts him with stones, but David refuses to let Abishai kill him, accepting the cursing as possibly from the LORD. In Jerusalem, Hushai wins Absalom's trust, and Ahithophel advises Absalom to sleep with his father's concubines in public, which he does on the palace roof.
story: The chapter moves back and forth between the fleeing king and the new king in the capital. On the road, David meets two men from Saul's world, one bringing gifts and one bringing curses, and both test his judgment. In Jerusalem, Absalom makes his break with his father public and irreversible. Nathan's prophecy in 12:11-12 is fulfilled almost word for word: another man lies with David's wives in broad daylight before all Israel, on the same palace roof from which David first saw Bathsheba (11:2). The stories of Ziba and Shimei are left open and return when David comes back in chapter 19; Shimei's end comes only in 1 Kings 2.
historical:
Bahurim was a village in the territory of Benjamin, just east of Jerusalem on the road down toward the Jordan. Shimei's family belonged to Saul's clan, and his curses show that the house of Saul still had supporters who saw David as a usurper. His charge that David had shed "the blood of the house of Saul" (verse 8) may refer to the deaths of Abner and Ish-bosheth (chapters 3-4), which David had publicly disowned, or to the execution of seven of Saul's descendants recorded in chapter 21, if that event took place earlier. Either way, the accusation shows how David's rise looked to Saul's kin.

Ahithophel's counsel was held in extraordinary regard. The narrator's comment that it was "like the consultation of the word of God" (verse 23) explains why David feared his defection so much and why his prayer in 15:31 mattered so greatly.
cultural:
Taking a king's concubines was a public claim to his throne. A concubine was a wife of secondary status, and the royal harem belonged to the reigning king. Abner's relations with Saul's concubine were taken as a political move (3:7), and Solomon later treated Adonijah's request for David's companion Abishag as a bid for the throne (1 Kings 2:22). Absalom's act was meant to make reconciliation impossible, so that his followers would not fear being abandoned in a deal between father and son. Ahithophel says so directly: Absalom must become a stench to his father.

Cursing was taken seriously in the ancient world; a curse was a spoken wish for harm, often invoking God. Throwing stones and dust was both an insult and a threat. Abishai's phrase "dead dog" (verse 9) is the same insult Mephibosheth once used of himself (9:8). David's response, "What have I to do with you, O sons of Zeruiah?" is an idiom of sharp disagreement, distancing himself from his nephews' violence.
literary: The chapter is built on contrasts. Ziba brings bread and wine; Shimei brings stones and curses. Hushai speaks loyal-sounding words with double meaning (he says he will serve "the one chosen by the LORD" without saying who that is); Ahithophel gives counsel of cold political calculation. David's reaction to Shimei is the spiritual center. He refuses to answer violence with violence and reads the curse as possibly permitted or even sent by the LORD, then hopes that God will see his affliction and repay him with good. The chapter's closing note on Ahithophel prepares for the contest of counsel in chapter 17.

outline.t: Ziba's gifts and his charge against Mephibosheth
David restrains Abishai and accepts the cursing
Ahithophel's counsel and Absalom on the roof

doctrines.note: David believes that even Shimei's curses might come under God's sovereign permission: "the LORD has told him so." He does not treat the curse as a mere accident or a thing to be crushed, but as something within God's purposes that he must bear.
David accepts humiliation as possibly deserved and entrusts himself to God, hoping for good in return. The chapter shows a way to receive unjust or partly just accusations without retaliating.
Nathan's words that David's wives would be taken in broad daylight are fulfilled on the palace roof. The consequences of hidden sin are made public.

words.note: Qalal, to curse, from a root meaning to be light or slight. To curse someone is to treat them as of no weight, to wish them diminished. Shimei's curses occur seven times in the chapter. In the Abrahamic promise God said he would curse the one who curses Abraham (Genesis 12:3), and David leaves such judgment to God.

Beliyyaal, worthlessness, often rendered worthless or wicked. Shimei calls David a worthless man of bloodshed (verse 7). The word marks someone as morally corrupt, and in later Jewish writing and in the New Testament Belial becomes a name for Satan (2 Corinthians 6:15).

Dam, blood. Shimei's charge that David is a man of blood (verses 7-8) is partly false and partly true. David did not kill Saul or his heirs, but he did shed Uriah's blood, and the reader knows it. Shimei's curse hits a mark he may not have intended.
Etsah, counsel. Ahithophel's counsel here is effective and ruthless. The narrator compares it to consulting the word of God, which sets up the drama of chapter 17, when God himself will defeat it.

christ: David's response to Shimei anticipates a pattern the New Testament makes central. When cursed, he did not curse in return; he entrusted himself to God. Peter describes Jesus in similar terms: when he was reviled, he did not revile in return, but kept entrusting himself to the one who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). Like David, Jesus left Jerusalem across the Kidron and faced mockery. The difference is decisive: David accepted curses he partly deserved, while Jesus bore curses he did not deserve, becoming a curse for us, in Paul's words (Galatians 3:13). The link is a pattern of response, not a prediction, but it helps show what kind of king the son of David would be.

hard.q: Did God really tell Shimei to curse David?
hard.a: David says, "the LORD has told him so" (verse 11), and interpreters read the claim in different ways. Some take it as David's humble recognition that God rules all things, including the malice of others, so that even an enemy's curses can be used by God to discipline him, without making God the author of Shimei's sin. Others take it as a statement of David's uncertainty (the preceding verse begins with "If") and his resolve to leave judgment to God rather than to act on his own. In either case, David does not approve Shimei's behavior; later he asks Solomon to deal with Shimei (1 Kings 2:8-9). The chapter's lesson is not that every curse comes from God but that David, humbled by his own sin, chose to bear this one rather than add to the bloodshed.

questions: David made a quick judgment about Mephibosheth based on Ziba's story. How can you avoid making decisions on one-sided information?
David chose not to retaliate against Shimei. When have you been tempted to answer an insult with force?
Absalom's act was designed to make reconciliation impossible. What actions in relationships burn bridges, and how can they be avoided?
